Tabulate and compare categories

Source: vignettes/tabulation.Rmd
tabulation.Rmd

The course coordinator wants to know whether participants were satisfied, and whether the two centres tell the same story. Start with a frequency table, then choose the layout that answers each follow-up question. Results remain ordinary tables that work with dplyr.

Start with one question

These are the same twelve participants used in Getting started, keeping only the columns needed here.

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidystata)

survey <- tribble(
  ~id, ~centre,     ~satisfied,
    1, "Riverside", "Yes",
    2, "Riverside", "Yes",
    3, "Riverside", "No",
    4, "Riverside", NA,
    5, "Riverside", "Yes",
    6, "Riverside", "Yes",
    7, "Hilltop",   "No",
    8, "Hilltop",   "Yes",
    9, "Hilltop",   "No",
   10, "Hilltop",   "Yes",
   11, "Hilltop",   "Yes",
   12, "Hilltop",   NA
)

survey |> tab(satisfied)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   satisfied     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 No            3    25    25      30        30
#> 2 Yes           7    58.3  83.3    70       100
#> 3 NA            2    16.7 100      NA        NA

Seven participants said yes, three said no, and two did not answer. Read the columns in terms of the question you want to answer:

Column Question
n How many participants gave this answer?
percent What percentage of all twelve participants is that?
valid What percentage of the ten who answered is that?
cum, valid_cum What percentage have we reached in the displayed order?

All four percentage columns use a 0-100 scale. Thus the yes share is 58.3% of everyone and 70% of respondents. Missing categories have no valid percentage. Cumulative percentages are most useful for categories with a meaningful order.

Choose joint, separate or cross-tabulated counts

The three tab functions answer different questions using the same columns.

Which combinations occur?

tab() counts combinations in one long table. With two columns, each row is a centre-answer combination:

survey |> tab(centre, satisfied)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   centre    satisfied     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>     <chr>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   No            2   16.7   16.7    20        20
#> 2 Hilltop   Yes           3   25     41.7    30        50
#> 3 Riverside No            1    8.33  50      10        60
#> 4 Riverside Yes           4   33.3   83.3    40       100
#> 5 Hilltop   NA            1    8.33  91.7    NA        NA
#> 6 Riverside NA            1    8.33 100      NA        NA

Here percent and cum use all twelve participants; valid and valid_cum use the ten with both centre and satisfaction observed. Adding a third variable would count three-way combinations.

What is each variable’s distribution?

tab1() makes separate one-way tables. Use .type = "tibble" to stack them into one table with a variable column:

survey |> tab1(centre, satisfied, .type = "tibble")
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   variable  value         n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>     <chr>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 centre    Hilltop       6    50    50      50        50
#> 2 centre    Riverside     6    50   100      50       100
#> 3 satisfied No            3    25    25      30        30
#> 4 satisfied Yes           7    58.3  83.3    70       100
#> 5 satisfied NA            2    16.7 100      NA        NA

Each variable has its own denominator. The default instead returns a named list, convenient when the tables will be used separately.

How do the centres compare side by side?

tab2() puts the second variable’s categories in columns. Cells contain counts, rather than the percentages from tab():

survey |> tab2(centre, satisfied)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   `centre \\ satisfied`    No   Yes  `NA`
#>   <chr>                 <int> <int> <int>
#> 1 Hilltop                   2     3     1
#> 2 Riverside                 1     4     1

With more than two selected variables, tab2() returns a list of tables for every pair, rather than one higher-dimensional table. Use .flip = TRUE to exchange rows and columns.

Compare percentages within each centre

To compare satisfaction rates, put the centre in .by instead of counting it as another measured variable:

survey |> tab(satisfied, .by = centre)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   centre    satisfied     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>     <chr>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   No            2    33.3  33.3    40        40
#> 2 Hilltop   Yes           3    50    83.3    60       100
#> 3 Hilltop   NA            1    16.7 100      NA        NA
#> 4 Riverside No            1    16.7  16.7    20        20
#> 5 Riverside Yes           4    66.7  83.3    80       100
#> 6 Riverside NA            1    16.7 100      NA        NA

Both centres have six participants and five observed answers. Riverside’s yes share is 80% of respondents; Hilltop’s is 60%. The missing answers still appear, so the difference between all-participant and valid shares stays visible.

One-way and joint tables also inherit group_by() groups:

survey |>
  group_by(centre) |>
  tab(satisfied) |>
  filter(satisfied == "Yes") |>
  select(centre, n, percent, valid)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   centre        n percent valid
#>   <chr>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop       3    50      60
#> 2 Riverside     4    66.7    80

The result is ungrouped. An explicit .by replaces inherited groups. tab2() and fre2() require an explicit .by to make separate cross-tables by group; group_by() alone does not split their results.

Add totals and readable labels

fre() adds total rows. Here we encode the answer to illustrate imported numeric categories with value labels:

labelled <- survey |> mutate(answer_code = encode(satisfied))

labelled |> fre(answer_code)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   answer_code     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>       <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 No              3    25    25      30        30
#> 2 Yes             7    58.3  83.3    70       100
#> 3 Valid Total    10    83.3  NA     100        NA
#> 4 NA              2    16.7 100      NA        NA
#> 5 Total          12   100    NA      NA        NA

tab() retains stored category codes and types; fre() displays value labels. Distinct codes remain distinct even when they share a label. fre1() adds totals to separate one-way tables; fre2() adds row and column totals to a cross-tabulation:

survey |> fre2(centre, satisfied)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   `centre \\ satisfied`    No   Yes  `NA` total
#>   <chr>                 <int> <int> <int> <int>
#> 1 Hilltop                   2     3     1     6
#> 2 Riverside                 1     4     1     6
#> 3 total                     3     7     2    12

fre2() displays labels for row categories; column headers retain category codes. You can also request totals with .total = TRUE in the tab family. Totals are useful for presentation, but use tables without total rows for further arithmetic so observations are not counted twice.

Order and reuse the results

Which answer is most common? .desc = TRUE sorts by decreasing count, keeping missing values last:

survey |> tab(satisfied, .desc = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   satisfied     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>     <int>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Yes           7    58.3  58.3    70        70
#> 2 No            3    25    83.3    30       100
#> 3 NA            2    16.7 100      NA        NA

Factors follow their level order by default; other categories sort by value. .group_order = "frequency" separately orders group blocks by their totals. Use dplyr to keep the categories relevant to a report:

survey |>
  tab(satisfied, .by = centre) |>
  filter(!is.na(satisfied)) |>
  arrange(centre, desc(n)) |>
  select(centre, satisfied, n, valid)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   centre    satisfied     n valid
#>   <chr>     <chr>     <int> <dbl>
#> 1 Hilltop   Yes           3    60
#> 2 Hilltop   No            2    40
#> 3 Riverside Yes           4    80
#> 4 Riverside No            1    20

Filtering here keeps the percentages already calculated. To change a denominator, filter the source observations before calling tab(). Empty strings count as observed answers, so clean blank text first if it means nonresponse.

Count a file that already contains frequencies

Suppose a second coordinator sends an aggregate file: one row represents several people. Use the frequency column as .wt:

register <- tribble(
  ~satisfied, ~people,
  "Yes",           7,
  "No",            3,
  NA,              2
)

register |> tab(satisfied, .wt = people)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   satisfied     n percent   cum valid valid_cum
#>   <chr>     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 No            3    25    25      30        30
#> 2 Yes           7    58.3  83.3    70       100
#> 3 NA            2    16.7 100      NA        NA

This reproduces the individual-level table. Frequency weights sum to the reported counts. Analytic weights (.wt_type = "analytic") instead rescale weights within each group to its number of rows; their percentages agree, but their counts have a different interpretation. Missing weights exclude rows, and negative weights are invalid. These options do not account for a complex survey design.

Association tests and longer tables

For an association test, .chi2 = TRUE adds Pearson’s chi-square and Cramer’s V. Remove missing answers first when nonresponse should not enter the test:

association <- survey |>
  filter(!is.na(satisfied)) |>
  tab2(centre, satisfied, .chi2 = TRUE)
#> Pearson chi2(1) = 0.4762   Pr = 0.490
#> Cramer's V = 0.2182

The test is reported as a message. Its numerical results are also available on the returned table:

attr(association, "chi2")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   statistic    df p_value cramers_v     n
#>       <dbl> <int>   <dbl>     <dbl> <int>
#> 1     0.476     1   0.490     0.218    10

This tiny teaching sample has small expected cell counts, so use the example to learn the interface, rather than draw an inference about the programme. Analytic weights are not supported for this test.

Score variables can produce long tables because every distinct value is counted. Add the first assessment item from our survey and shorten its display with a one-time printer, which still returns every row:

survey |>
  mutate(score = c(2, 4, NA, 6, 8, 4, 3, 5, 7, 9, NA, 6)) |>
  tab(score) |>
  print_interval(n = 6)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 6
#>   score     n percent    cum valid valid_cum
#>   <dbl> <int>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1     2     1    8.33   8.33    10        10
#> 3     4     2   16.7   33.3     20        40
#> 4     5     1    8.33  41.7     10        50
#> 6     7     1    8.33  66.7     10        80
#> 7     8     1    8.33  75       10        90
#> 9    NA     2   16.7  100       NA        NA
#> # ... 3 rows omitted between displayed positions; use print(x, n = Inf) to show
#> # all rows.

For formatted reports, the fre family supports .type = "flextable" when that optional package is installed. See the output conventions for lists and table classes, or continue to measurement summaries.
